status_summary: EPA revisited the 2024 designation of PFOA and PFOS as CERCLA hazardous substances and kept it: in a 2025-09-17 court filing in the Chamber of Commerce challenge, EPA said it had finished its review and would keep the listing, would begin a section 102(a) rulemaking on a framework for future designations, and would address passive receiver liability within current authority while a full fix needs Congress. EPA's 2026-02-06 year-one release again lists the affirmation of the listing, and on 2026-08-18 the D.C. Circuit denied all petitions in Chamber of Commerce v. EPA, No. 24-1193, leaving the designation in place. No proposed rule for the section 102(a) framework, no passive receiver rulemaking, no proposal to remove the designation and no revision of the groundwater cleanup rules for PFAS was found in a systematic check on 2026-10-18. Separately, on 2026-05-20 EPA proposed to extend the compliance deadline for the PFOA and PFOS drinking water limits from 2029-04-26 to 2031-04-26 for systems that request it.

timeline.event: EPA Administrator announces plans (month only given; first of month used) to work with Congress and industry on a liability framework that protects passive receivers that did not make or generate PFAS.

In a court filing in the Chamber of Commerce's challenge, EPA states it has finished its review and will keep the 2024 designation of PFOA and PFOS as CERCLA hazardous substances; it also announces a planned rulemaking under CERCLA section 102(a) for a framework to designate future hazardous substances and says a statutory fix on passive receiver liability needs Congress (law firm summaries).
EPA's year-one PFAS release lists the affirmation of the CERCLA hazardous substance listing for PFOA and PFOS among its actions; it names no other PFAS designations.

EPA proposes (91 FR, doc. 2026-10086) an exemption extending the PFOA and PFOS drinking water compliance deadline from 2029-04-26 to 2031-04-26 for systems that request it; this is under the Safe Drinking Water Act, not CERCLA.

The D.C. Circuit unanimously denies the petitions for review in Chamber of Commerce v. EPA, No. 24-1193, upholding the designation of PFOA and PFOS as CERCLA hazardous substances; law firm summaries note possible rehearing or Supreme Court review.
